Bedbug concerns have resurfaced on Southeastern trains after reported insect sightings led to six service cancellations. Find out what the operator says.


## Bedbug Concerns Resurface on Southeastern Railway Services


Fresh concerns about suspected bedbugs on Southeastern railway services have emerged after reports of insects allegedly crawling between passenger seats prompted disruption to six train services connecting Kent and London.


According to reports published on October 17, 2026, the latest incident involved a Southeastern train operating from Slade Green Depot in Bexley. The suspected sightings have raised questions about passenger comfort, railway cleanliness and the measures being taken to investigate potential pest problems.


However, the claims remain disputed. Southeastern has denied that bedbugs have been found in passenger areas, stating that specialist contractors have not identified the insects in spaces used by travellers.


## Reported Sightings Lead to Railway Disruption


The latest concerns reportedly began when insects were spotted on a Southeastern train associated with Slade Green Depot. Images described in media reports allegedly showed a reddish insect moving between two passenger seats.


An internal email cited in reporting reportedly referred to a member of train crew raising concerns after three suspected bedbugs were seen near a poster by a carriage door. An internal record also allegedly described an infestation after an off-duty member of staff reported the discovery.


Following the reports, the train was suspended as it arrived at Dartford. The decision reportedly contributed to knock-on disruption, with six services between Kent and London cancelled.


Carriages suspected of being affected were subsequently kept out of service while checks were carried out.


Although these reports have attracted attention, the presence of bedbugs in passenger seating has not been confirmed by the train operator. Southeastern maintains that inspections have not found bedbugs in areas used by passengers.


## More Suspected Insects Reported on the Network


The latest incident follows a series of reported bedbug sightings involving Southeastern services since September 22.


Previous concerns have reportedly involved train carriages, drivers' cabs and staff belongings. Some drivers have expressed concerns about working conditions and the possibility of insects being transported between railway locations.


Reports have also described two carriages being taken out of service following suspected sightings. In another alleged incident, a driver reportedly requested protective equipment because of concerns about possible exposure.


These accounts have contributed to the nickname "Bedbug Express" appearing in coverage of the controversy.


Nevertheless, it is important to distinguish between suspected sightings and verified infestations. An insect seen on a train is not necessarily a bedbug, and identification by a qualified pest control professional is important before conclusions can be drawn.


## What Has Southeastern Said About the Claims?


Southeastern has firmly disputed suggestions that its passenger trains are experiencing a confirmed bedbug infestation.


The company's managing director, Steve White, reportedly stated that two driver cabs out of approximately 800 had received treatment, alongside furniture at a depot.


The operator has also said that suspected insects identified during previous reports were found to be other types of insects.


David Wornham, Southeastern's customer experience director, expressed disappointment at continued reports suggesting that bedbugs were present across the railway network.


According to the reported statement, specialist contractors had found no bedbugs in areas used by passengers, despite several suspected sightings. The company said this remained the position at the time of its response.


These statements highlight the difference between concerns raised by staff and passengers and the findings reported by the operator's inspection teams.


Further verified information would be needed to establish whether the latest reports involve confirmed bedbugs, another type of insect or an isolated incident.


## Union Calls for Passenger and Staff Reassurance


The reported incidents have also prompted concerns about the wellbeing of railway employees and the confidence of passengers.


Maryam Eslamdoust, general secretary of the Transport Salaried Staffs' Association, said passengers should not have to worry about taking bedbugs home after travelling. She also stressed that railway workers deserve to feel safe in their workplaces.


The union representative called for prompt action, thorough cleaning of affected carriages and professional pest treatment where necessary.


Clear communication is also important when suspected pests are reported. Staff need a reliable process for raising concerns, while passengers need accurate information about inspections, cleaning procedures and any necessary service changes.


Where a potential pest problem is identified, a structured response can help prevent unnecessary disruption and provide reassurance without making claims that have not been verified.


## Can Bedbugs Spread Through Public Transport?


Bedbugs are small insects that feed on human blood. They commonly hide in seams, crevices, upholstered furniture, mattresses and other sheltered spaces.


Although they are often associated with beds and bedrooms, bedbugs can also be transported in luggage, clothing and personal belongings. Public transport environments may provide opportunities for accidental transfer when insects or eggs are carried on items brought aboard.


However, the possibility of transport does not mean that every suspected sighting indicates an established infestation.


Bedbugs do not normally live on people in the same way as lice. They tend to hide in suitable spaces and may be transported between locations through belongings.


Passengers concerned about possible exposure can take sensible precautions, including inspecting luggage and clothing after a suspected encounter and avoiding placing bags on visibly affected upholstery.


If a traveller has a credible reason to suspect that their belongings have been exposed, they can seek advice from a reputable pest control professional about appropriate inspection and treatment options.


## What Should Passengers Do Next?


Travellers using Southeastern services should follow official service updates before setting off, particularly if they rely on routes connecting Kent with London.


If passengers spot an insect they believe may be a bedbug, they should report it to railway staff and provide a description or photograph where it is safe and practical to do so. They should avoid handling the insect directly.


Anyone concerned about a possible exposure should inspect their belongings calmly rather than assuming that an infestation has occurred. Professional identification is the most reliable way to determine whether an insect is a bedbug.


Passengers should also remember that service cancellations may result from precautionary inspections and operational decisions. A cancellation alone does not establish that bedbugs have been confirmed in a carriage.


## Conclusion: Questions Remain Over Southeastern Bedbug Reports


The latest reports of suspected bedbugs on Southeastern trains have renewed concerns about railway cleanliness, staff safety and passenger reassurance. Six services were reportedly cancelled following the latest incident, adding to the attention surrounding previous suspected sightings.


However, Southeastern continues to deny that bedbugs have been found in passenger areas, citing inspections by specialist contractors. The available reports therefore do not establish that an infestation has been confirmed on the network.


For now, passengers should rely on verified updates from Southeastern and report any suspected sightings through the appropriate channels. Transparent communication, accurate insect identification and professional pest management will be essential to addressing concerns and maintaining public confidence.


### Disclaimer


This article is for general informational purposes only. The reported bedbug sightings have not been independently verified for this article, and Southeastern disputes claims that bedbugs have been found in passenger areas. Details may change as further information becomes available. Readers should consult Southeastern's official announcements for the latest service information and confirmed findings.
